title: Two views of a failed replication
bodyMd:
**Passage A**

A scientific result becomes credible when independent investigators can reproduce it. If a reported effect disappears in a carefully repeated study, confidence in the original claim should fall. Researchers sometimes respond by naming subtle differences between the settings. Such differences may matter, but they cannot be invoked merely to protect a favored result from every possible test. A claim compatible with both the presence and absence of an effect, without prior limits, has little explanatory content. The issue is not whether the original investigators acted honestly. A sincere observation can be unstable, and an honest explanation can still be too accommodating. Scientific criticism concerns the relationship between a claim and possible evidence, not merely the character of the person who advances it. Investigators should be able to describe an outcome that would count against their revised account. Without that commitment, adding conditions after each failure can make a theory increasingly elaborate while leaving its evidential risk unchanged.

The remedy is to specify the conditions under which the effect is expected and test those conditions prospectively. If temperature is said to matter, vary temperature deliberately. If participant experience is said to matter, state how it will be measured before looking at outcomes. Failed replication can improve a theory, but only when the proposed explanation generates a new opportunity to be wrong.

**Passage B**

Replication is indispensable, yet the phrase “the same study” can hide important choices. A social intervention may depend on an institution's history, on participants' expectations, or on the meaning of a task in a particular setting. Repeating the visible procedure elsewhere need not reproduce those conditions. A failed effect can reveal the boundary of a mechanism rather than the nonexistence of the mechanism.

This possibility is not a license for retrospective excuses. Contextual explanations should identify observable differences and make predictions about new settings. The investigator who says only that each place is unique explains nothing. But treating every failure as a simple verdict of falsity is equally unhelpful. The task is to distinguish an unreliable effect from an effect whose scope was described too broadly, and that distinction requires new comparative evidence.
